         The Office of Public Utility Counsel (OPUC), representing the interests of residential and

small commercial consumers in Texas, respectfully submits these comments on the Public Utility

Commission of Texas’s (PUCT or Commission) Proposal for Publication of Amendments to 16

Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.192, relating to Transmission Rates for Export from Electric

Transmission Cost Recovery Factors (TCRF); and new 16 TAC § 25.252, relating to Large Load

Customer Tariffs (Proposal for Publication or PFP). 1 The PFP requests public comment by August

11, 2026, which OPUC has timely met. 2

                                        I. GENERAL COMMENTS

        The majority of transmission projects recently endorsed by ERCOT are primarily driven

to serve large load customers. 3 OPUC appreciates the Commission’s efforts to take measures that

better assign the transmission costs caused by large load customers are paid for by these customers

through a combination of the proposed 12 Coincident Peak (12CP) and minimum billing demand

(MBD) charge. Although these two methods do not go far enough to completely shift large load

customers’ share of transmission costs away from residential and small commercial consumers,

they are a significant improvement from the current system. To prevent potential weakening of the

cost recovery mechanisms to the detriment of residential and small commercial consumers, the

recommendations included in these comments are focused on aspects of the proposed rule intended

to bring about changes that are robust, effective, and consistent with the Commission’s cost

causation principle.

                                II. COMMENTS ON PFP QUESTIONS

PFP Question 1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand
provisions be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

        Transmission is built to serve the large load customer at 100% contracted peak demand,

not its NCP, average demand, or any lesser amount of the large load’s contracted capacity. The

cost to construct transmission is not based solely on a customer’s demand size, peak or NCP. Other

factors, such as geographical differences, rights of way, voltage ride-through capability, and

preexisting grid infrastructure, can influence transmission construction and associated costs.




        3
           “Texas may overhaul power market to handle data center boom,” by Shelby Webb, E&E News by
POLITICO, (Mar. 26, 2026), https://www.eenews.net/articles/texas-may-overhaul-power-market-to-handle-data-
center-boom/ (last visited Aug. 11, 2026) (quoting PUCT Chairman Gleeson that “a lot of this [transmission] build –
the majority of it – is for these large industrial data center customers.”).

                                                        4
 Therefore, all large load customers should be subject to the same MBD provision regardless of the

individual load’s contracted peak demand or NCP. If the Commission chooses to use varied MBD

provisions for large load customers with different contracted peak demand amount or different

NCP demands, it must include a recovery mechanism that precludes transmission costs accrued by

large loads to serve large loads at their contracted demand from shifting to other ratepayers,

including residential and small commercial consumers.

PFP Question 2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be: (a) fixed for 20 years as
proposed; (b) reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or (c) extended to a longer period
of time?

       The MBD should be extended to a longer time period that more closely aligns with the

useful life of transmission assets, which generally range from 40 to 50 years. This would be

consistent with ratemaking principles adopted in other jurisdictions where the contract term is tied

to the depreciable life of the associated infrastructure. If the Commission determines that a longer

MBD obligation is not feasible, OPUC urges the Commission to keep the 20-year fixed period.

Using a shortened or reduced MBD time frame increases transmission investment costs caused by

large load customers that will ultimately shift to residential, small commercial, and other

consumers.

       If the Commission elects to adopt an MBD period of fewer than 20 years, the Commission

should incorporate accelerated depreciation into the large load cost recovery framework. Requiring

large loads to pay a greater portion of their transmission-related costs during the earlier years of

service reduces the risk that their share of costs is shifted to residential and small commercial

customers and other ratepayers, especially if the large load breaks the contract, ceases operations

or goes bankrupt prior to the end of the 20-year contract period. Accelerated depreciation is




                                                 5
 particularly important if the Commission lowers upfront financial collateral requirements or if the

transmission is built to serve customers in higher-risk industries.

       Alternatively, the Commission could apply accelerated depreciation as an additional cost

recovery method to high-risk large load customers that do not have proven economic development,

creditability, and local community and labor investment.

PFP Question 3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure
of demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the
large load minimum billing demand:
    (a) reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
        some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
        demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in phases
        over the years, and how?
    (b) be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large load
        minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load customer’s
        contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous year and the large
        load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage weighting towards
        contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases over the years, and how?

       No to the overall Question 3, as well as to Questions 3a. and 3b.

       There is a possibility that a large load customer will neither ramp up on schedule nor

completely use the demand capacity originally included in the interconnection agreement, whether

in phases or upon complete energization. Thus, under both the “ratcheted” demand and “weighted

average” methods, large load customers would pay less than the total amount of transmission costs

the utility accrued to build the infrastructure necessary to serve the loads at the large load

customer’s fully contracted capacity.

       With the “ratcheted” demand and “weighted average” methods, the billing determinants

(denominator) in the minimum billing demand formula are reduced, which would lower the

amount of transmission costs recovered from the large load customers. As a result, both the

ratcheted demand and weighted average approaches would lead to shifting payment of

transmission costs accrued by the large load customer from that customer onto other ratepayers.



                                                 6
 Residential and small commercial consumers, who have a much smaller electric footprint and

pocketbook, should not foot the million- or billion-dollar transmission bill created by large load

customers’ interconnection to the grid.

       If the Commission desires to incorporate a ratcheted demand or weighted average method,

then it is recommended that these be implemented after the contracted period is over (currently 20

years in the existing PFP language). If used prior to then, the two methods would allow large loads

to “free ride” on the backs of everyday Texans.

PFP Question 4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load,
defined as an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists
of power electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable legal
support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational loads.

       As long as the separate treatment does not result in non-electronic based large load

customers’ transmission costs being shifted to residential and small commercial consumers, OPUC

would be amenable to separate rate treatment for large computational loads in which 50% or

greater of the demand at the site of interconnection consists of power electronic based load.

     Both conventional and electronic based large load customers require transmission

infrastructure to interconnect and access power from the ERCOT grid. Both types of large load

customers cause significant transmission costs to accrue in order to serve them. Consequently, for

both types of large load customers, residential and small commercial consumers should not

subsidize their accumulated transmission costs. Separate rate treatment of electronic based large

load customers where they alone, and not conventional large loads, are subject to the same MBD

provisions, then residential and small commercial consumers could end up paying for conventional

large load customers’ transmission costs if no additional cost recovery method is established.




                                                  7
         For example, a chemical plant applies to interconnect to the ERCOT grid at 100 megawatts

(MW), subjecting them to proposed large load interconnection standards in Project No. 584814

and this project. The chemical plant is approved, and the interconnecting utility starts building the

transmission to interconnect the plant at the contracted capacity of 100MW. Despite the contracted

capacity, on average, the chemical plant operates at 80MW. Under the existing PFP language, the

chemical plant must pay a minimum billing demand for all 100MW for 20 years even though the

plant would often operate at 80MW. The minimum billing demand protects transmission costs

built for the plant’s other 20MW from shifting to other consumer classes for the life of the 20-year

contract.

        However, if the minimum billing demand is removed from non-electronic based large load

customers, the chemical plant’s transmission costs would be based on 12CP alone. Given the

chemical plant’s load factor, the plant likely will not be operating at 100MW during all of the

12CP intervals. Thus, under 12CP, the chemical plant would not pay for all of the transmission

costs it caused with its 100MW interconnection. Instead, difference between the large load

customer’s contracted demand and 12CP demand would be shifted onto other rate payers,

including everyday Texans.

        Although conventional large load customers do not pose the same risk factors as electronic

based large load customers, they still require transmission infrastructure to serve them. If large

load customers do not pay for the interconnection costs they caused to be created, electronic based

or not, those costs have to be paid by someone. That someone would be other consumer classes,

which includes residential and small businesses. Therefore, even if a separate rate class is created




        4
             Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA 37.0561, Project No. 58481
(pending).



                                                        8
 for electronic based large load customers, there must be cost recovery mechanisms put in place

other than 12CP to ensure the conventional large load customers’ transmission costs are not paid

for by residential and small commercial consumers.

     If a separate rate class is created for electronic based large load customers, there are certain

questions that would need to be answered:

            Would conventional or non-electronic based large load customers be subject to a
             minimum billing demand charge? If not, who would pay for the transmission costs
             accrued by these large load customers?

            Would non-electronic based large load customers have their costs allocated solely
             using 12CP? If so, how would the costs be shifted if the non-electronic based large
             load customer primarily operated at an average demand lower than their contracted
             capacity?

            What mechanisms would be in place to ensure that other customers, especially
             residential and small commercial consumers, are not subsidizing large industrial
             customers’ transmission costs? In other words, what cost recovery method would the
             Commission put in place to ensure the transmission costs accrued to serve the
             non-electronic based large load customers at 100% contracted capacity are not passed
             on to other ratepayers, particularly residential and small commercial consumers?

       Electronic based large load customers may present a higher risk of early departure or

reduced operations compared to conventional load customers. Conventional industrial customers,

such as manufacturing plants, refineries, and steel mills, often represent long-established

businesses with significant investments in physical infrastructure, employees, and local

communities. These customers generally have longer operating histories and lower business risk,

making a longer MBD obligation appropriate. In contrast, large electronic loads like data centers

operate in a rapidly evolving industry that is more susceptible to changes in technology, AI

demand, finance conditions, and broader market forces. Many of these types of electronic-based

businesses do not have decades-long operating histories, and the facilities themselves typically

employ relatively few workers compared to conventional industrial facilities. The Commission




                                                 9
 could consider imposing additional consumer protections on these high-risk large load customers

without lessening the cost recovery mechanisms in the proposed PFP.

PFP Question 5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened
to include transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       Yes, with a true-up mechanism to allow for adjustments after the conclusion of the 90-day

Refinement Study.

       The definition of transmission interconnection costs should include all transmission

projects identified at the conclusion of the initial six-month batch study process, prior to the

commencement of the 60-day commitment window. There is a possibility that all of the large load

customers undergoing a batch study commit to connect at the capacity allocated at the end of the

batch study. In that scenario, there would be no changes to the transmission infrastructure needed

to serve the load, because all of the customers contract to interconnect at the demand amount

previously studied in the batch load. A broad definition also ensures that any upfront financial

commitments reflect the anticipated costs associated with connecting large loads to the ERCOT

system and reduces the risk that residential and small commercial consumers will ultimately bear

costs that are primarily attributable to large load customers’ interconnection request and awarded

capacity.

       OPUC recognizes that after the 60-day commitment period, there is a possibility that not

all large load customers awarded capacity will choose to interconnect. Accordingly, the

Commission should establish a true-up mechanism that allows transmission interconnection costs

and any associated financial commitments or MBD obligations to be adjusted following

completion of the Refinement Study. If the Refinement Study determines that fewer transmission

facility upgrades are necessary, the interconnecting load would receive a reduction or credit as




                                               10
 appropriate. Conversely, the Refinement Study may identify additional transmission upgrades,

including upstream facilities that were not included in the initial batch study estimates. In that

scenario, the large load customer’s financial commitment and MBD should be adjusted upwards

to reflect those additional transmission costs.

PFP Question 6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective
of whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how
should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
transmission planning studies?

       Resource Adequacy. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity

regardless of their ability to achieve full energization, a base case should encompass the customer’s

full contracted peak demand in resource adequacy reports and assessments. The inherent nature of

a resource adequacy assessment is to plan for the worst-case scenario, when all customers are

consuming power at their peak demand, to ensure there is sufficient generation to meet grid

demand. If a large load customer consistently uses energy below their contracted capacity, future

resource adequacy reports could include a sensitivity analysis that models that behavior along with

the primary base case scenario that reflects full contracted peak demand.

       Transmission Planning. If large load customers are able to reserve capacity, the

Commission should ensure that these loads fully pay for the transmission build out to serve the

load at their reserved capacity, irrespective of the customer’s actual energy usage. During the

transmission planning process, the primary justification for new or upgraded transmission

infrastructure is to serve the new large load customer at its contracted peak demand on the bulk

system. Therefore, the Commission should ensure that all associated transmission costs are fully

paid for by the large load customer the infrastructure was built to serve.

       If, during the interconnection agreement, the large load customer requests to reduce its

demand capacity to be significantly lower than the original contracted demand amount, the large



                                                  11
 load still should pay for any transmission investment already built to serve that large load customer

at the original contracted demand amount.

        Given the rapidly changing nature of the operational technology employed by electronic

based loads, there is a very real possibility that emergent technology could significantly reduce the

energy needs of these loads. 5 As a result, the amount of transmission needed to serve them today

could be much lower in the next several years. The reduced transmission need would incentivize

the large load customer to substantially decrease their contracted capacity under the existing

interconnection agreement. Under this scenario, the Commission should establish a process that

allows loads to reduce their contracted capacity demand while simultaneously requiring the load

pays for any transmission infrastructure already built to serve the load’s originally allocated

contracted capacity. Without such a guardrail, other customer classes, including residential and

small commercial consumers, will be left paying for transmission built specifically to serve loads

that no longer require or use it.

                   III. COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSED RULE LANGUAGE

    A. Apply 12CP over a consecutive 12-month period.

        OPUC strongly supports the PFP’s current definition of the ERCOT 12CP intervals:

        “ERCOT 12CP intervals -- The set of 12 30-minute intervals composed of the ERCOT
        system monthly peak demand interval for each of the 12 calendar months from October 1
        of one year through September 30 of the subsequent year, inclusive.” 6




         5

Enables Data Centers to Operate Without Utility Power, No External Water Use, Low Noise, Low Energy Use and

https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/new-system-enables-data-centers-to-operate-without-utility-power-no-
external-water-use-low-noise-low-energy-use-and-ninety-percent-carbon-capture-302846310.html (last visited Aug.
11, 2026).
        6
            PFP at 10 (citing 16 TAC § 25.192(b)(4)).



                                                        12
             The PFP’s definition ensures that other values informed by the ERCOT 12CP intervals

take into consideration peak demand values from each calendar month. Any change to this

definition, specifically one that allows for floating 12CP intervals, where multiple intervals are

permitted to occur in the same month, will result in significant cost-shifting, likely reverting to

something similar to the existing 4CP method, and harm residential and small commercial

customers.

            A floating 12CP model would allows for intervals to cluster during naturally occurring

peak demand events, such as heat waves or winter storms. This creates an incentive for the same

“sophisticated large industrial consumers” that “can reasonably predict 4CP intervals and rapidly

reduce consumption during likely peak hours” 7 to curtail during the floating 12CP intervals, which

may be easier to predict than a single interval once a month over a 12 consecutive month period.

            OPUC conducted an analysis to see the impact a floating 12CP method would have on

residential consumers compared to a consecutive month 12CP method and the existing 4CP

method. For a floating 12CP model, six floating intervals were selected during the summer months

of June through September, four floating intervals during the winter months of December through

February, and two intervals during the shoulder months. 8 Fifteen-minute intervals were used, with

one interval peak per day. OPUC’s analysis found that under 4CP, the average residential share of

transmission costs for the ERCOT region for 2025 through 2030 is forecast to be 35.1%. 9 Under

the floating 12CP method used, the residential share decreased less than half a percentage point

with approximately $16 million yearly in cost savings for residential consumers. In contrast, using




            7

4, 2026).
            8
                The shoulder months used in the particular analysis for the floating 12CP model were April and October.
            9

                                                             13
 the consecutive month 12CP method,10 residents’ share of transmission costs dropped to 31.3%

resulting in yearly cost savings of approximately $211 million for residential consumers. The

complete analysis can be found in Appendix A.

        Therefore, OPUC strongly recommends the Commission keep the PFP’s current definition

of ERCOT 12CP intervals to protect residential and small commercial consumers and other

ratepayers, as well as achieve the Commission’s original objective to implement Senate Bill 6 by

transitioning from a 4CP to a 12CP method to more appropriately allocate transmission investment

costs to the customers that causes them.

    B. No back-end incentive exists for large load customers to maintain operations after
       receiving the financial security refund in Project 58481 but before the end of the 20-
       year contract.

        The current PFP contains no back-end incentive for a large load customer to comply with

the MBD period for the full 20-year contract period.

        Under the existing language in Project No. 58481, after outstanding costs are paid, a large

load customer that fully energizes will receive a complete refund of the remaining balance of their

financial security [excluding Contributions in Aid of Construction (CIAC) and the interconnection

fee] after meeting the final milestone of phased energization of its contracted peak demand.” 11

Similarly, a fully energized large load customer will receive a complete refund of the remaining




        10
             The months used to analyze the consecutive month 12CP period were October 1 through September 1.
         11
            Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561, Project No.
58481, Proposal for Publication at 29 (Mar 12, 2026). (citing proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(i)(1); “After applying
financial security to any outstanding amounts owed, the interconnecting [distribution service provider] or . . .
[transmission service provider] must refund 20% of the remaining balance when the large load customer energizes
and ratably as the large load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
energization of its contracted peak demand.” (emphasis added)) (Project No. 58481 PFP).

 balance of their financial security (excluding CIAC and the interconnection fee) after “sustaining

operations for five years at the customer’s contracted peak demand.” 12

         After energizing at the final phase or sustaining operations for five years, the large load

customer has no financial incentive to stick around for another 15 years to finish paying the higher

portion of their share of transmission costs they caused to be created. Consequently, large load

customers may choose to halt their business operations in Texas and move elsewhere once they

receive their financial security refund from the interconnecting utility. 13 A utility could sue the

large load customer for breach of contract in court, but legal costs for doing so may outweigh the

benefit. In this scenario, and assuming the utility satisfies the recovery requirements, the large

load’s remaining transmission costs would be shifted on to other consumers—including residential

and small commercial consumers.

         Adding a termination fee would be a back-end door incentive to encourage the large load

customer to continue operations and pay the minimum billing demand charge for the duration of

the 20-year contract. This type of fee has been included in proposed or adopted contracts or tariffs

involving large load customer interconnection in roughly 19 other states. 14

         The termination fee would be limited to those large load customers that break the contract

prior to the end of the 20-year period. The fee would cover the amount of transmission costs

remaining as if the large load customer would continue operating at the site of interconnection.




         12
             Project No. 58481 PFP at 29 (citing proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(i)(2); The rule language is not clear if a
large load customer that energizes in phased milestones must also sustain operations for five years prior to receiving
the refund).
         13

No. 58481 PFP at 29 (citing proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(i)).
         14

Alliance and NC Clean Energy Technology Center “DELTAa: Database of Emerging Large-Load Tariffs” (August
2026), available for download at https://sepapower.org/large-load-tariffs-database/



                                                           15
 Any amounts the interconnecting utility recovered from the large load customer under the

termination fee would be applied to offset transmission costs in the same manner as if the large
